summary: Describes the vendor information extensions of the Bootstrap Protocol, which let a BOOTP server hand a booting machine extra settings such as a subnet mask or gateway address. It revises RFC 1048. It was replaced by RFC 1533.

eli5.summary: When a computer starts up it knows nothing. This memo lists the extra notes a helper can hand over, such as where the nearby router is.

questions: what extra information can bootp send
what is the bootp magic cookie
how big is the bootp vendor field
subtitle: A tagged list of settings a BOOTP server can hand to a booting machine in the 64-byte vendor field.

tldr.problem: BOOTP gives a booting host an address and a boot file, but its last field, a 64 octet vendor area, had no common meaning, so servers could not hand out useful settings in a uniform way.
tldr.mechanism: The area starts with a 4 octet magic cookie, 99.130.83.99, followed by tagged fields such as subnet mask (tag 1), gateway (tag 3) and domain name server (tag 6), ended by tag 255.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1497 is a Draft Standard that revised RFC 1048 and added tag 18. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 1533.

today: RFC 1497 is a Draft Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 1533, so that is the document to read for current definitions. It obsoleted RFC 1048, RFC 1084 and RFC 1395, and it updates RFC 951.

sections.title: Why BOOTP Needs Extensions
sections.content:
The Bootstrap Protocol (BOOTP) is a UDP/IP-based protocol that lets a booting host configure itself dynamically and without user supervision. It can assign an IP address, name a file to download a boot program from, name the server holding it and, if present, give the address of an Internet gateway.

RFC 1497 is a slight revision and extension of RFC 1048, credited to Philip Prindeville, and it introduces Tag 18 for Extension Path. It defines a potentially vendor-independent interpretation of the vendor information area of the BOOTP packet, so that one server can serve mixed clients at a site with a generic class of data.

The memo also explains how it fits with RFC 903 (RARP), which assigns an IP address to a hardware address but provides only part of the functionality needed.
sections.eli5: Imagine a new kid at school who is handed a name tag and a room number. This memo adds extra notes to that handout, like where the playground is and who the teacher is.

sections.title: The Vendor Information Field
sections.content:
The memo concerns only the last field of the BOOTP packet, a 64 octet area reserved for vendor information. Its first four bytes are the magic cookie, which says how the rest is to be read. The value is the 4 octet dotted decimal 99.130.83.99 (hexadecimal 63.82.53.63) in network byte order.

After the cookie comes a free-format run of tagged sub-fields. Most are length tagged, so a client that does not understand a tag can skip it. Lengths do not count the tag and length octets, and all multi-byte quantities are in network byte order.

Fixed length fields come in two shapes: a lone tag octet with no data (implicit length of one octet), or a tag octet, a length octet and that many data octets. Variable length fields always use the tag, length, data shape.
sections.eli5: The field starts with a secret password that says 'the notes that follow use this system'. Each note then has a label and a size, so a reader can skip a note it does not understand.

sections.title: The Defined Tags
sections.content:
The fixed fields are Pad (tag 0, no data, used to align later fields to word boundaries), Subnet Mask (tag 1, 4 bytes, which must precede the gateway field if present), Time Offset (tag 2, 4 bytes, a signed 32-bit number of seconds from UTC) and End (tag 255, marking the end of usable data; the rest should be filled with pad octets).

Variable length fields mostly carry lists of IP addresses, N bytes for N/4 servers: Gateway (3, with the preferred one first), Time Server (4), IEN-116 Name Server (5), Domain Name Server (6), Log Server (7), Cookie/Quote Server (8), LPR Server (9), Impress Server (10) and RLP Server (11).

Others carry text or numbers: Hostname (12), Boot File Size (13, a two octet count of 512 octet blocks), Merit Dump File (14), Domain Name (15), Swap Server (16, one address), Root Path (17) and Extensions Path (18).

Extensions Path names a file, retrievable via TFTP, that is read like the 64-octet vendor field except that its length is unconstrained and any Tag 18 inside it is ignored. Tags 128 to 254 are reserved for site-specific use and should follow all data using the generic tags 0 to 127.
sections.eli5: Each label means one thing: 'your neighbourhood mask', 'where the router is', 'who tells the time', 'what your name is'. A label called END says there are no more notes.

sections.title: Adding New Tags and Staying Within 64 Bytes
sections.content:
New generic fields are registered with the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA). Using undefined generic types in the range 19 to 127 without registration may conflict with other implementations.

Space is tight. The memo says care should be taken not to exceed the 64 byte length restriction. Nonessential information such as the host name and the quote of the day server can be left out and found later with a more appropriate service, such as RLP or the WKS resource-type of the domain name system.
sections.eli5: The note card is small. If it is full, leave off the unimportant notes and ask someone else for them later.

sections.title: Comparison to Alternative Approaches
sections.content:
A section contributed by Steve Deering argues that extending BOOTP may not be necessary. Instead of each host module asking the BOOTP server for server addresses, each could multicast directly to the server group it needs, possibly with expanding ring multicasts.

The memo lists three advantages of multicast: it removes dependency on a BOOTP server that may be unavailable or have an incorrect database, it reduces the chore of keeping a replicated BOOTP database consistent, and it can reduce packet traffic or delay. It also notes the BOOTP approach is uniform and gives an administrator easy control over which hosts use which servers.

The main drawback of multicast is that IP multicasting is not widely implemented and existing services do not understand it. The BOOTP approach may be most efficient when a single BOOTP reply carries everything the client needs.
sections.eli5: You could ask one helper for all the answers, or you could shout the question and let whoever knows reply. Each way has good and bad points, and the memo lists them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo states that security issues are not discussed in it. A booting client simply takes the settings that arrive in the reply.
sections.eli5: The memo does not talk about how to stop someone from handing out wrong notes.
